chunks: "For a prototype I design for change and observability instead of cost or size.
First, I make it easy to see: test points on every rail, clock, reset and key signal, with ground pads next to them, plus status LEDs and a debug header.
Second, I make it easy to change.

Anywhere I'm unsure, a feedback divider, a filter corner, a compensation network, a gain setting, I add extra footprints so I can try different values without cutting anything, or I use a trim pot or a jumper to switch options.
I put 0 ohms links in series with power domains so I can power or measure one block at a time, and strap options on boot pins.
Third, I break out spare pins from the MCU or FPGA to a header, so if I find I need another signal I can wire it.
I use larger, hand-solderable parts, 0603 or 0805 instead of 0201, wherever space allows, and leave room around ICs for rework, and I put clear silkscreen net names.
I'd keep the stack-up and traces conservative so any fab can make it, and use sockets for the expensive or likely-to-change parts.
I still follow DFM basics, because a prototype that can't be assembled doesn't teach me anything, and I order a few extra boards."
